title: ProMo3D: Probing Motion Cues in Frozen 3D Foundation Models
claim: A frozen foundation model plus a tiny trained probe yields dense outputs, beating heavier supervised decoders with less data and capacity.
layout: 5 stages left-to-right with block arrows; bottom comparison banner
description: A left-to-right pipeline. On the far left, a film strip of dance video frames sits under a box that lists the training set (160 YouTube-VOS videos) and the held-out test sets. Block arrows lead to a blue rounded box labeled 'Frozen 3D foundation model', with a snowflake icon and stacked options π³X, VGGT, DA3 and 'etc.' joined by 'or'. The next box, 'Probe', shows colored input tokens passing through a tall orange projection bar to blue and red output tokens. Then a 3D scatter plot of blue static and red dynamic points shows the discriminative subspace. The last panel, 'Output motion', has an orange border. It stacks a rainbow heatmap score map, a coarse binary mask, and a SAM2-refined mask. A bottom banner compares against GeoMotion on less data, a smaller model and better performance, each with an icon.
caption: Overview of Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD). Given an input frame group, a frozen feed-forward 3D foundation model such as π3X [36], VGGT [34], or Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [21] produces token representations. A lightweight probe trained on only 160 videos maps these features into a probe-induced static–dynamic discriminative representation. PMD then converts anchor-based pairwise probe scores into dense dynamic score maps, which are thresholded into coarse masks and optionally refined with SAM2 [29]. It transfers zero-shot to DAVIS [26, 27], SegTrackv2 [17], and FBMS-59 [14], while requiring substantially less training data and trainable capacity than high-capacity motion decoders such as GeoMotion [8].
abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models have recently reshaped multi-view reconstruction, yet dynamic 4D understanding still often relies on large-scale motion supervision or hand-crafted, architecture-specific heuristics. We ask whether frozen 3D foundation model tokens already encode motion-relevant information that can be exposed by lightweight readout functions, rather than re-learning motion-specific features with high-capacity decoders. Through probing on three representative backbones, we find that static--dynamic separation is decodable from frozen token representations. Our rank-restricted and spectral analyses on $Ï^3$X reveal that the recovered motion cues are concentrated in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this, we propose Probing-based Motion Distillation (PMD), which converts pairwise motion-state compatibility scores against a fixed anchor token into dense motion masks. Trained on only 160 YouTube-VOS videos using a single 16 GB GPU, PMD transfers zero-shot to DAVIS, SegTrackv2, and FBMS-59 without target-benchmark fine-tuning. With multi-view pretrained geometric backbones, PMD outperforms training-free heuristics and approaches substantially heavier supervised and self-supervised methods, suggesting that motion decoding from frozen 3D foundation models can be lightweight and data-efficient.
